abstract: Most bacterial cells have at least one class A penicillin-binding protein (aPBP) that plays a key role in cell wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis. It is generally assumed that peptidoglycan synthesis activity constitutes the primary, if not the only, function of aPBPs. Loss of PBP1, the major aPBP of Bacillus subtilis, results in a mild morphogenic phenotype in which cells are thinner and longer than normal. The increased length was thought to be responsible for an increase in the number of nucleoids per cell. However, we now show that ponA mutants, which lack PBP1, have a chromosome segregation defect. The defect appears to occur because the reduced cell diameter impacts chromosome architecture. The increased cell length probably arises because the chromosome abnormality occludes cell division sites. The main consequence of the altered chromosome arrangement seems to be a specific defect in chromosome segregation, characterized by increased chromosome dimer formation, as inactivation of the XerCD-dif system in ponA mutants leads to severe chromosome segregation and growth defects. Restoring cell width by combining ponA with an mreB mutation suppresses the chromosome segregation defect. These results demonstrate that cell architecture has an important influence on chromosome organization and dynamics.
